abstract:
State-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms typically use random sampling (e.g., $\epsilon$-greedy) for exploration, but this method fails on hard exploration tasks like Montezuma's Revenge. To address the challenge of exploration, prior works incentivize exploration by rewarding the agent when it visits novel states. Such intrinsic rewards (also called exploration bonus or curiosity) often lead to excellent performance on hard exploration tasks. However, on easy exploration tasks, the agent gets distracted by intrinsic rewards and performs unnecessary exploration even when sufficient task (also called extrinsic) reward is available. Consequently, such an overly curious agent performs worse than an agent trained with only task reward.  
Such inconsistency in performance across tasks prevents the widespread use of intrinsic rewards with RL algorithms. We propose a principled constrained optimization procedure called Extrinsic-Intrinsic Policy Optimization (EIPO) that automatically tunes the importance of the intrinsic reward: it suppresses the intrinsic reward when exploration is unnecessary and increases it when exploration is required. The results is superior exploration that does not require manual tuning in balancing the intrinsic reward against the task reward. Consistent performance gains across sixty-one ATARI games validate our claim. The code is available at https://github.com/Improbable-AI/eipo.

# Reconciling intrinsic rewards via constrained policy optimization

Anonymous Author(s)

Affiliation

Address

email

# Abstract

The use of intrinsic rewards in policy optimization via reinforcement learning has led to impressive performance gains on several hard exploration Atari games such as Montezuma's Revenge. However, recent studies show that intrinsic rewards can bias the policy optimization and cause worse performance than optimizing only the environment reward in most tasks other than hard exploration ones. Such inconsistent performance prevents the use of intrinsic rewards with RL algorithms on a general set of tasks. We propose using constrained policy optimization to eliminate the detrimental effects of intrinsic rewards while preserving their merits when applicable. Experimental results across 61 Atari games validate our claim. The end result is a superior exploration algorithm that does not require manual tuning to trade intrinsic rewards against extrinsic rewards.

# 1 Introduction

Exploration-exploitation is at the core of reinforcement learning (RL) [1]. The central challenge of exploration-exploitation is to balance the time spent discovering better policies (exploration) and taking greedy actions to maximize rewards (exploitation). In the absence of methods that work well in both theory and practice, state-of-the-art methods rely on strategies such as adding a small amount of noise to actions or randomly sampling a suboptimal action with small probability (e.g.,  $\epsilon$ -greedy). However, such strategies fail on notoriously hard exploration tasks such as the Atari game Montezuma's Revenge where the rewards are sparse [2]. In sparse reward scenarios, non-zero rewards are infrequent which hinders policy improvement.

A popular approach for solving hard exploration tasks is to supplement the environment (or the extrinsic) reward  $(r_{E})$  with an exploration bonus (or intrinsic reward  $r_I$ ) generated by the agent itself [3-5, 2, 6]. Intrinsic rewards encourage the agent to visit novel states and thus increase the chance of visiting states that yield extrinsic rewards. Many prior works [6, 2, 7] show that jointly optimizing intrinsic and extrinsic rewards (i.e.,  $r_E + \lambda r_I$ , where  $\lambda \geq 0$  is a hyperparameter) instead of only optimizing the extrinsic reward (i.e.  $\lambda = 0$ ) improves performance on hard exploration tasks.

Despite success on hard exploration tasks such as Montezuma's Revenge, a recent study found that using intrinsic rewards does not consistently outperform simple exploration strategies such as  $\epsilon$ -greedy across Atari games [8]. Whitney et al. [9] suggest that intrinsic rewards can degrade performance due to the bias they introduce in the policy optimization objective. Jointly maximizing intrinsic and extrinsic rewards does not necessarily yield the optimal policy with regard to extrinsic rewards alone.

Fig. 1a illustrates this intuition with the help of a toy example. Here the green triangle is the agent, and blue/pink circles denote the location of extrinsic and intrinsic rewards, respectively. Maximizing the sum of intrinsic and extrinsic rewards can lead the learned policy to move right along the bottom corridor and therefore be suboptimal with respect to the extrinsic rewards which are located at the

# 2 Preliminaries

top. In such a scenario, better performance will be obtained if the agent only optimizes the extrinsic reward. The trouble, however, is that a priori one does not know how to trade off (i.e., choose  $\lambda$ ) intrinsic v/s extrinsic rewards.  
A common practice is to find the best  $\lambda$  using an extensive hyperparameter search. The problem is that different values of  $\lambda$  are adept for different tasks (see Fig. 4). Furthermore, as the agent progresses on the task, the exploration-exploitation trade off can vary. In the initial absence of extrinsic rewards, exploration is preferred. Once enough extrinsic rewards are obtained, the agent might prefer exploitation of these rewards instead of exploration. The exact dynamics of the exploration-exploitation trade off are task-dependent, and per-task tuning is tedious, undesirable and often computationally infeasible.  
We present an exploration strategy that alleviates the need to manually tune the relative importance of extrinsic and intrinsic rewards. Our method leverages the bias of intrinsic rewards when it is useful for exploration and mitigates this bias when it does not lead to an increase in extrinsic rewards. This is achieved using an extrinsic optimality constraint that forces the extrinsic rewards earned by the joint policy to be equal to those earned by the optimal policy with respect to the extrinsic rewards. Directly optimizing this constraint in general settings is intractable because the optimal extrinsic reward is unknown. We devise a practical algorithm which we call Extrinsic-Intrinsic Policy Optimization (EIPO) that uses an approximation to solve this constrained optimization problem (Section 3).  
While in principle we can apply EIPO to any intrinsic reward method, we evaluate performance using the state-of-the-art, random network distillation (RND) [7]. Fig. 1b presents teaser results on two ATari games: (i) Montezuma's revenge on which joint optimization with RND (red) substantially outperforms a PPO policy [10] optimized with only extrinsic rewards (black); (ii) Jamesbond where PPO substantially outperforms RND. These results demonstrate that in some games the bias of intrinsic rewards helps, but in others it can hurt. In contrast, our algorithm EIPO (blue) matches the best algorithm in both games, showing that it can leverage intrinsic rewards as necessary. A large-scale study on all 61 ATari games reinforces this finding. Additionally, in some games EIPO outperforms multiple strong baselines with and without intrinsic rewards, indicating that our method both mitigates performance degradation resulting from intrinsic reward bias and improves performance beyond the current state-of-the-art.  
We consider a discrete-time Markov Decision Process (MDP) consisting of a state space  $S$ , an action space  $\mathcal{A}$ , and an extrinsic reward function  $\mathcal{R}_E: S \times \mathcal{A} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ . Note that we distinguish the components for extrinsic and intrinsic rewards by  $E$  and  $I$ , respectively. The extrinsic reward function  $\mathcal{R}_E$  defines the objective of the task (e.g., game score). The agent starts from an initial state  $s_0$  sampled from the initial state distribution  $\rho_0: S \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ . At each timestep  $t$ , the agent perceives a state  $s_t$  of the environment, takes action  $a_t$  sampled from the policy  $\pi$ , receives extrinsic reward  $r_t^E = \mathcal{R}_E(s_t, a_t)$ , and moves to the next state  $s_{t+1}$  according to the transition function  $\mathcal{T}(s_{t+1}|s_t, a_t)$ . Our goal is to

use the experience of interactions with the environment to find the optimal policy  $\pi$  such that the extrinsic objective value  $J_{E}(\pi)$  is maximized:

$$
\max  _ {\pi} J _ {E} (\pi), \text {w h e r e} J _ {E} (\pi) = \mathbb {E} _ {s _ {0}, a _ {0}, \dots \sim \pi} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} r _ {t} ^ {E} \right] \tag {1}
$$

$$
s _ {0} \sim \rho_ {0}, a _ {t} \sim \pi (a | s _ {t}), s _ {t + 1} \sim \mathcal {T} (s _ {t + 1} | s _ {t}, a _ {t}) \forall t > 0
$$

The  $\gamma$  denotes a discount factor. For brevity, we abbreviate  $\mathbb{E}_{s_0,a_0,\dots \sim \pi}\left[\cdot \right]$  as  $\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\cdot \right]$  unless specified.

Curiosity-driven exploration methods [6, 7, 2] attempt to ease exploration by providing "intrinsic rewards" to the agent to encourage it to visit unseen states. With the intrinsic reward function  $\mathcal{R}_I: S \times \mathcal{A} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ , the optimization objective is:

$$
\max  _ {\pi \in \Pi} J _ {E + I} (\pi), \text {w h e r e} J _ {E + I} (\pi) = \mathbb {E} _ {\pi} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} \left(r _ {t} ^ {E} + \lambda r _ {t} ^ {I}\right) \right] (\text {M i x e d o b j e c t i v e}), \tag {2}
$$

where  $\lambda$  denotes the intrinsic reward scaling coefficient. We abbreviate intrinsic reward at timestep  $t$  as  $r_t^I = \mathcal{R}_I(s_t, a_t)$ . State-of-the-art curiosity-exploration strategies [7, 11] often optimize the objective in Eq. 2 using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [10]. Using PPO, we take trajectories  $\tau_{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}} := (s_0, a_0, r_0^E, s_1, a_1, r_1^E, \dots)$  generated by the current policy  $\pi_{\mathrm{old}}$  and intrinsic rewards  $(r_0^I, r_1^I, \dots)$  from an arbitrary  $\mathcal{R}_I$  to solve a new policy  $\pi$  for  $\max_{\pi \in \Pi} J_{E + I}(\pi)$ .  $\pi$  is then set as  $\pi_{\mathrm{old}}$  and used to sample trajectories for solving another new policy.

# 3 Mitigating the Bias of Intrinsic Rewards

Simply maximizing the sum of intrinsic and extrinsic rewards does not guarantee a policy that also maximizes the extrinsic reward. Formally, put  $\arg \max_{\pi_{E + I}}J_{E + I}(\pi_{E + I})\neq \arg \max_{\pi_E\in \Pi}J_E(\pi_E)$  At convergence, the optimal policy  $\pi_{E + I}^{*} = \arg \max_{\pi_{E + I}}J_{E + I}(\pi_{E + I})$  could be suboptimal w.r.t.  $J_{E}$  that defines the performance of a policy on the task. Because the performance of the agent is measured only based on extrinsic reward, we propose to enforce an extrinsic optimality constraint to ensure that the optimal "mixed" policy  $\pi_{E + I}^{*} = \arg \max_{\pi_{E + I}}J_{E + I}(\pi_{E + I})$  leads to as much extrinsic reward as the optimal "extrinsic" policy  $\pi_E^* = \arg \max_{\pi_E\in \Pi}J_E(\pi_E)$ . The resulting optimization objective is the following:

$$
\max  _ {\pi_ {E + I} \in \Pi} J _ {E + I} \left(\pi_ {E + I}\right) \tag {3}
$$

subject to  $J_{E}(\pi_{E + I}) - \max_{\pi_{E}}J_{E}(\pi_{E}) = 0$  (Extrinsic optimality constraint).

Solving this optimization problem can be viewed as proposing a policy  $\pi_{E + I}$  that maximizes  $J_{E + I}$ , and checking if the proposed  $\pi_{E + I}$  is feasible given the extrinsic optimality constraint.

The constrained objective is difficult to optimize because evaluating the extrinsic optimality constraint requires  $J_{E}(\pi_{E}^{*})$ , which is unknown. We show that this optimization problem can be solved by transforming it into an unconstrained min-max optimization problem using Lagrangian duality (Section 3.1). Next, we present an iterative algorithm for min-max optimization by alternating between maximization and minimization in Section 3.2 and an implementation in Section 3.3.

# 3.1 The Dual Objective: Unconstrained Min-Max Optimization Problem

The Lagrangian dual problem for the primal constrained optimization problem in Eq. 3 is:

$$
\min  _ {\alpha \in \mathbb {R}} \left[ \max  _ {\pi_ {E + I} \in \Pi} J _ {E + I} \left(\pi_ {E + I}\right) + \alpha \left(J _ {E} \left(\pi_ {E + I}\right) - \max  _ {\pi_ {E} \in \Pi} J _ {E} \left(\pi_ {E}\right)\right) \right], \tag {4}
$$

where  $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$  is the Lagrangian multiplier. We simplify Eq. 4 by merging  $J_{E + I}(\pi)$  and  $J_{E}(\pi)$ :

$$
J _ {E + I} ^ {\alpha} (\pi_ {E + I}) = J _ {E + I} (\pi_ {E + I}) + \alpha J _ {E} (\pi_ {E + I}) = \mathbb {E} _ {\pi_ {E + I}} \Big [ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} ((1 + \alpha) r ^ {E} (s _ {t}, a _ {t}) + r ^ {I} (s _ {t}, a _ {t})) \Big ].
$$

Substituting  $J_{E + I}^{\alpha}(\pi_{E + I})$  into Eq. 4 and rearranging terms yields the following min-max problem:

$$
\min  _ {\alpha \in \mathbb {R} ^ {+}} \left[ \max  _ {\pi_ {E + I} \in \Pi} \min  _ {\pi_ {E} \in \Pi} J _ {E + I} ^ {\alpha} \left(\pi_ {E + I}\right) - \alpha J _ {E} \left(\pi_ {E}\right) \right]. \tag {5}
$$

# 3.2 Algorithm for Optimizing the Dual Objective

We now describe an algorithm for solving  $\pi_{E + I},\pi_E$  , and  $\alpha$  in each of the subproblems in Eq. 5.

Extrinsic policy  $\pi_E$  (min-stage).  $\pi_E$  is optimized via the minimization sub-problem, which can be re-written as a maximization problem:

$$
\min  _ {\pi_ {E} \in \Pi} J _ {E + I} ^ {\alpha} \left(\pi_ {E + I}\right) - \alpha J _ {E} \left(\pi_ {E}\right)\rightarrow \max  _ {\pi_ {E} \in \Pi} \alpha J _ {E} \left(\pi_ {E}\right) - J _ {E + I} ^ {\alpha} \left(\pi_ {E + I}\right) \tag {6}
$$

The central challenge in this optimization is that evaluating objectives  $J_{E + I}^{\alpha}(\pi_{E + I})$  and  $J_{E}(\pi_{E})$  requires sampling trajectories from both policies  $\pi_{E + I}$  and  $\pi_{E}$  which is data inefficient. If the two policies are similar, we can perform the optimization using data collected only from  $\pi_{E + I}$  using the approximation proposed in [12]. To make this approximation we first use an identity from [13] to re-write the objective  $\alpha J_{E}(\pi_{E}) - J_{E + I}^{\alpha}(\pi_{E + I})$  as (see Appendix A.1 for detailed derivation):

$$
\alpha J _ {E} \left(\pi_ {E}\right) - J _ {E + I} ^ {\alpha} \left(\pi_ {E + I}\right) = \mathbb {E} _ {\pi_ {E}} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} U _ {\min } ^ {\pi_ {E + I}} \left(s _ {t}, a _ {t}\right) \right], \tag {7}
$$

where  $U_{\min}^{\pi_{E + I}}(s_t, a_t) \coloneqq \alpha r_t^E + \gamma V_{E + I}^{\pi_{E + I}}(s_{t + 1}) - V_{E + I}^{\pi_{E + I}}(s_t)$ ,

$$
V _ {E + I} ^ {\pi_ {E + I}} (s _ {t}) := \mathbb {E} _ {\pi_ {E + I}} \Big [ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} (r _ {t} ^ {E} + r _ {t} ^ {I}) | s _ {0} = s _ {t} \Big ].
$$

Now we can use the approximation from [12] to formulate Eq. 7 as:

$$
\mathbb {E} _ {\pi_ {E}} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} U _ {\min } ^ {\pi_ {E + I}} \left(s _ {t}, a _ {t}\right) \right] \approx \mathbb {E} _ {\pi_ {E + I}} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} \frac {\pi_ {E} \left(a _ {t} \mid s _ {t}\right)}{\pi_ {E + I} \left(a _ {t} \mid s _ {t}\right)} U _ {\min } ^ {\pi_ {E + I}} \left(s _ {t}, a _ {t}\right) \right] \tag {8}
$$

subject to  $\mathbb{E}_{s\sim \pi_{E + I}}\left[\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{E + I}(.|s)||\pi_{E}(.|s))\right]\leq \delta ,$

where  $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}$  denotes the Kullback-Leibler divergence and  $\delta$  is a small constant threshold that limits the divergence between two policies. Note that the expectation is computed with respect to data collected only from  $\pi_{E + I}$ . We solve for the new  $\pi_E$  by optimizing a clipped version of the objective in Eq. 8, similar to PPO. More details are provided in Appendix A.2.

Mixed policy  $\pi_{E + I}$  (max-stage). This subproblem of solving  $\pi_{E + I}$  is posed as

$$
\max  _ {\pi_ {E + I} \in \Pi} J _ {E + I} ^ {\alpha} \left(\pi_ {E + I}\right) - \alpha J _ {E} \left(\pi_ {E}\right). \tag {9}
$$

Similarly to solving  $\pi_E$  we use the approximation used in Eq. 8 to rewrite the objective  $J_{E + I}^{\alpha}(\pi_{E + I}) - \alpha J_{E}(\pi_{E})$  as follows (see Appendix A.1 for details):

$$
J _ {\alpha E + I} \left(\pi_ {E + I}\right) - \alpha J _ {E} \left(\pi_ {E}\right) \approx \mathbb {E} _ {\pi_ {E}} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} \frac {\pi_ {E + I} \left(a _ {t} \mid s _ {t}\right)}{\pi_ {E} \left(a _ {t} \mid s _ {t}\right)} U _ {\max } ^ {\pi_ {E}} \left(s _ {t}, a _ {t}\right) \right] \tag {10}
$$

subject to  $\mathbb{E}_{s\sim \pi_E}\Big[\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_E(.|s)||\pi_{E + I}(..|s))\Big]\leq \delta$

where  $U_{\max}^{\pi_E}(s_t,a_t)\coloneqq (1 + \alpha)r_t^E +r_t^I +\gamma \alpha V_E^{\pi_E}(s_{t + 1}) - \alpha V_E^{\pi_E}(s_t)$

$$
V _ {E} ^ {\pi_ {E}} (s _ {t}) := \mathbb {E} _ {\pi_ {E}} \Big [ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} r _ {t} ^ {E} | s _ {0} = s _ {t} \Big ].
$$

Lagrangian multiplier  $\alpha$ . Let  $g(\alpha) := \max_{\pi_{E + I} \in \Pi} \min_{\pi_E \in \Pi} J_{E + I}^{\alpha}(\pi_{E + I}) - \alpha J_E(\pi_E)$ . We solve  $\min_{\alpha} g(\alpha)$  using gradient descent with step size  $\beta$  as shown below (see Appendix A.1 for details):

$$
\alpha \leftarrow \alpha - \beta \nabla_ {\alpha} g (\alpha) \approx \alpha - \beta \mathbb {E} _ {\pi_ {E}} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} \frac {\pi_ {E + I} \left(a _ {t} \mid s _ {t}\right)}{\pi_ {E} \left(a _ {t} \mid s _ {t}\right)} r _ {t} ^ {E} + \gamma V _ {E} ^ {\pi_ {E}} \left(s _ {t + 1}\right) - V _ {E} ^ {\pi_ {E}} \left(s _ {t}\right) \right], \tag {11}
$$

subject to  $\mathbb{E}_{s\sim \pi_E}\Big[\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_E(.|s)||\pi_{E + I}(..|s))\Big]\leq \delta$

# 3.3 Implementation

Min-max alternation schedule We use an iterative optimization scheme that alternates between solving for  $\pi_E$  by minimizing the objective in Eq. 6, and solving for  $\pi_{E + I}$  by maximizing the objective in Eq. 9. Typically, min-max optimization switches between minimization and maximization stages at every iteration. We find that switching in each iteration hinders the performance of our method. We hypothesize that frequently switching leads to insufficient training for each policy, and thus we use the objective value between two subsequent iterations to determine when to switch. At each iteration, trajectories are collected using one of the two policies, and the other policy is trained using these trajectories. Let  $J[i]$  be the objective value  $J_{E + I}^{\alpha}(\pi_{E + I}) - \alpha J_{E}(\pi_{E})$  at iteration  $i$ . We switch the stage when the objective value does not improve anymore. The switching rule can be summarized as:

```latex
\[
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} J[i] - J[i - 1] \leq 0 \Rightarrow \text{max stage} \leftarrow \text{False}, \quad \text{if max stage} = \text{True} \\ J[i] - J[i - 1] \geq 0 \Rightarrow \text{max stage} \leftarrow \text{True}, \quad \text{if max stage} = \text{False}, \end{array} \right.
\]
```

where max stage is a binary variable indicating whether the current stage is max-stage. When max-stage is done,  $\alpha$  is updated using Eq. 11.

Parameter sharing In an image state space (e.g., Atari) it is preferable to share the convolutional neural network (CNN) backbone between  $\pi_E$  and  $\pi_{E + I}$  for the sake of data efficiency. However, if the backbone is shared, maximizing the objective (Eq. 9) over  $\pi_{E + I}$  could decrease  $\alpha J_{E}(\pi_{E})$  and impede the performance of  $\pi_E$  due to gradient interference in the shared backbone. Similarly, minimizing the objective (Eq. 6) over  $\pi_E$  could decrease  $J_{E + I}^{\alpha}$  and degrade the performance of  $\pi_{E + I}$  as well. To prevent such interference, we jointly optimize both  $\pi_{E + I}$  and  $\pi_E$  with additional auxiliary objectives  $\max_{\pi_{E + I}}J_{E + I}(\pi_{E + I})$  and  $\max_{\pi_E}J_E(\pi_E)$  during the min-stage and max-stage, respectively. Intuitively, the auxiliary objective compensates against gradient interference by introducing a counteracting force that attempts to fix the objective not being directly optimized during the current stage. For example, when maximizing  $J_{E + I}^{\alpha}(\pi_{E + I}) - \alpha J_{E}(\pi_{E})$  over  $\pi_{E + I}$ , the auxiliary objective  $\max_{\pi_E}J_E(\pi_E)$  can prevent any updates from decreasing  $J(\pi_E)$ .

In summary, we outline the practical policy optimization algorithm, Extrinsic-Intrinsic Policy Optimization (EIPO), for solving Eq. 5 in Algorithm 1. The detailed version is presented in Algorithm 2 in the Appendix. Note that we solve the constrained problem (Eq. 10 and Eq. 8) using a PPO-based approach. The full implementation details, including hyperparameters can be found in Appendix A.2.

Algorithm 1 Extrinsic-Intrinsic Policy Optimization (EIPO)  
1: Initialize policies  $\pi_{E + I}$  and  $\pi_E$ , max_stage[0]  $\leftarrow$  False, and  $J[0] \leftarrow 0$   
2: for  $i = 1 \cdots$  do ▷  $i$  denotes iteration index  
3: if max_stage[i - 1] then ▷ Max-stage: rollout by  $\pi_E$  and update  $\pi_{E + I}$   
4: Collect trajectories  $\pi_E$  using  $\pi_E$  and compute  $U_{\max}^{\pi_E}(s_t, a_t) \forall (s_t, a_t) \in \tau_E$   
5: Update  $\pi_{E + I}$  by Eq. 10 and  $\pi_E$  by auxiliary objective (Section 3.3)  
6:  $J[i] \leftarrow J_{E + I}^{\alpha}(\pi_{E + I}) - \alpha J_E(\pi_E)$   
7: max_stage[i]  $\leftarrow J[i] - J[i - 1] \leq 0$   
8: else ▷ Min-stage: rollout by  $\pi_{E + I}$  and update  $\pi_E$   
9: Collect trajectories  $\pi_{E + I}$  using  $\pi_{E + I}$  and compute  $U_{\min}^{\pi_{E + I}}(s_t, a_t) \forall (s_t, a_t) \in \tau_{E + I}$   
10: Update  $\pi_E$  by Eq. 8 and  $\pi_{E + I}$  by auxiliary objective (Section 3.3)  
11:  $J[i] \leftarrow J_{E + I}^{\alpha}(\pi_{E + I}) - \alpha J_E(\pi_E)$   
12: max_stage[i]  $\leftarrow J[i] - J[i - 1] \geq 0$   
13: end if  
14: if max_stage[i - 1] = True and max_stage[i] = False then  
15: Update  $\alpha$  (Eq. 28) ▷ Update when the max-stage is done  
16: end if  
17: end for

# 4 Experiments

We evaluate our method in 61 Atari games from the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) [14] benchmark, as well as Pycolab environments [15] for illustrative examples. We compare against the following baselines, where the text inside the parentheses denotes the acronym.

- PPO [10]: The policy is trained using PPO with extrinsic rewards only:  $\pi^{*} = \arg \max_{\pi \in \Pi} J_{E}(\pi)$ .  
- RND [7]: The policy is trained using PPO with the sum of extrinsic rewards  $r_t^E$  and intrinsic rewards  $\lambda r_t^I$  generated by RND:  $\pi^* = \arg \max_{\pi \in \Pi} J_{E + I}(\pi)$ .  
- Ext-norm-RND (EN): We propose a variant of RND where the extrinsic rewards are normalized using running mean and standard deviation (Appendix A.2). We include this as a baseline since our empirical results show that extrinsic reward normalization improves over RND in games where vanilla RND performs much worse than PPO.  
- Decay-RND (DY): We propose a variant of Ext-norm-RND where intrinsic rewards are progressively scaled down to eliminate exploration bias over time. Intrinsic rewards  $r_t^I$  are scaled by  $\lambda(i)$ , where  $i$  denotes the iteration number. The objective function turns into  $J_{E + I} = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t (r_t^E + \lambda(i)r_t^I)\Big]$ , where  $\lambda(i)$  is defined as  $\lambda(i) = \mathrm{clip}\left(\frac{i}{I} (\lambda_{\max} - \lambda_{\min}), \lambda_{\min}, \lambda_{\max}\right)$ , where  $\lambda_{\max}$  and  $\lambda_{\min}$  denote the predefined maximum and minimum  $\lambda(i)$ , and  $I$  is the iteration after which decay is fixed. We follow the linear decay schedule used to decay  $\epsilon$ -greedy exploration in DQN [16].  
- Decoupled-RND (DC) [17]: We adapt the method proposed in [17] to Ext-norm-RND. Two policies  $\pi_{E + I}$  and  $\pi_E$  are trained as follows:

$$
\pi_ {E + I} ^ {*} = \underset {\pi_ {E + I}} {\arg \max } \mathbb {E} _ {\pi_ {E + I}} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} \left(r _ {t} ^ {E} + r _ {t} ^ {I}\right) - \mathrm {D} _ {\mathrm {K L}} \left(\pi_ {E} | | \pi_ {E + I}\right) \right], \pi_ {E} ^ {*} = \underset {\pi_ {E}} {\arg \max } \mathbb {E} _ {\pi_ {I}} \left[ \sum_ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} \gamma^ {t} r _ {t} ^ {E} \right].
$$

The exploration policy  $\pi_{E + I}$  collects trajectories for training  $\pi_{E + I}$  and  $\pi_E$ .  $\pi_{E + I}$  and  $\pi_E$  maximize mixed and extrinsic objectives, respectively. The  $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_E||\pi_{E + I})$  term in the objective incentivizes  $\pi_I$  to perform differently from  $\pi_E$ .

Our method EIPO is implemented using Ext-norm-RND. The policies  $\pi_{E + I}$  and  $\pi_E$  are parametrized by two separate multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) with a shared CNN backbone. The value functions  $V_{E + I}^{\pi_E + I}$  and  $V_{E}^{\pi_E}$  are represented in the same fashion, and share the same CNN backbone with both policy networks. The hyperparameters and implementation details are described in the Appendix A.2. Note that while we chose to use RND due to it's state-of-the-art performance in hard exploration Atari games, our method is applicable to any bonus-based exploration method.

# 4.1 Illustrative example

We exemplify intrinsic reward bias using a simple navigation environment shown in Fig. 2a which illustrates a task with conflicting intrinsic and extrinsic rewards. The white sprite denotes the agent, which observes a  $5 \times 5$  window view of it's surroundings. If it reaches the (red) location at the top of the map, an extrinsic reward is provided. The (blue and magenta) blocks are randomly placed in the bottom corridor at the start of each episode. Because these blocks randomly change location, they induce RND intrinsic rewards throughout the course of training. Because intrinsic rewards along the bottom corridor are easier to obtain than the extrinsic reward, optimizing the mixed objective  $J_{E + I}$  can yield a policy that results in the agent exploring the bottom corridor (i.e., exploiting the intrinsic reward) without ever discovering the extrinsic reward at the top. Fig. 2b plots the evolution of the average extrinsic returns for PPO, RND, and EIPO across 5 random seeds during training. We find that EIPO outperforms both RND and PPO. RND gets distracted by colored blocks and underperforms compared to vanilla PPO. Notably, PPO performs slightly worse than EIPO, possibly because the extrinsic reward at the top cannot be trivially found without the guidance of intrinsic rewards.

We hypothesize that EIPO aggressively explores early on during training, and then focuses on exploiting extrinsic rewards after discovering the red location. To validate this hypothesis, we plot the average  $\alpha$  parameter, which controls the importance of extrinsic optimality of EIPO at each training iteration in Fig. 2c. It can be seen that  $\alpha$  decreases in the beginning, before increasing after the extrinsic return starts rising in Fig. 2b. This observation corroborates our hypothesis that EIPO is able to dynamically leverage intrinsic rewards for exploration while ultimately achieving high extrinsic returns.

# 4.2 Does EIPO generally improve PPO performance?

We validate whether EIPO prevents the possible performance degradation introduced by intrinsic rewards, and consistently either improves or matches the performance of PPO in 61 Atari games. As our goal is to investigate if an algorithm generally performs better than PPO, rather than measuring raw performance we evaluate each algorithm using the "probability of improvement" (Appendix A.4) metric suggested in [18]. We ran at least 5 random seeds for each method in each environment, collecting the median extrinsic returns within the last 100 episodes and calculating the probability of improvement  $P(A \geq \mathrm{PPO})$  with  $95\%$ -confidence interval against PPO for each algorithm  $A$ . The confidence interval is estimated using the bootstrapping method. Fig. 3a shows the probability of improvement for each method against PPO:  $P(A > \mathrm{PPO}) \forall A \neq \mathrm{PPO}$ . It can be seen that RND is the least likely to improve PPO, suggesting that RND does not yield consistent performance improvements across all 61 Atari games. Ext-norm-RND achieves a higher probability of improvement than RND, which suggests that normalizing extrinsic rewards improves the performance degradation of RND. Decay-RND has higher probability of improvement than Ext-norm-RND. This indicates that decaying the scale of intrinsic rewards over time is also a viable method to alleviate the performance drop of RND in Atari tasks, with the notable drawback that the decay schedule has to be tuned beforehand. Decoupled-RND attains a probability of improvement that is higher than RND yet lower than both Ext-norm-RND and Decay-RND. EIPO exhibited the highest probability of improvement among all the baselines, which shows that EIPO is more likely to improve the performance of PPO across Atari games.

In addition, Fig. 3c shows the percentage of Atari games in which one method matches or exceeds the performance of another method with a pairwise comparison. Note that "percentage of games  $A \geq B$ "  $R(A, B)$  is not equivalent to probability of improvements  $P(A \geq B)$ . Let  $\mu_A$  be the mean score of algorithm  $A$  over 5 random seeds in an environment.  $R(A, B)$  is defined as:  $R(A, B) = \frac{1}{N} [\mu_A \geq \mu_B]$  where  $N$  denotes the number of Atari games. The last row of Fig. 3c shows that EIPO performs better than all the baselines in the majority of games (i.e.,  $R(\text{EIPO}, B) > 0.5$ ).

# 4.3 Does EIPO perform better than the baselines?

As all our baselines improve upon vanilla RND, we compare EIPO with each baseline pairwise in terms of "strict probability of improvement". Strict probability of improvement  $P(A > B)$  (Appendix A.4.1) measures the likelihood that an algorithm  $A$  is strictly better than an algorithm  $B$ . Fig. 3b shows  $P(EIPO-RND > B) \forall B$ . It can be seen that EIPO outperforms all the baselines by more than  $50\%$ . As suggested in [18],  $P(EIPO-RND > B) > 0.5$  with a confidence interval less than 0.5 indicates that a result has statistical significance. We can therefore conclude that EIPO will generally perform better than all other baselines across all 61 Atari games.

# 4.4 Does EIPO preserve the performance gain of RND?

Surprisingly, EIP0-RND yields a higher performance gain than RND does, which implies that EIPO not only mitigates the bias introduced by intrinsic rewards in Atari games, but can also improve performance.

# 4.5 Does EIPO outperform tuned RND?

We empirically find that the performance of RND is heavily dependent on the difference in magnitude between  $r^{E}$  and  $r^{I}$ . Because this difference can be controlled through the intrinsic scaling coefficient  $\lambda$  and the best scaling coefficient is not known a priori, we tune  $\lambda$  for RND in several games where RND substantially under-performs compared to PPO in order to see if EIP0 can match or outperform the strongest tuned baseline. A variety of  $\lambda$  values are selected for each environment based on the relative difference in magnitudes between intrinsic rewards  $r^{I}$  and extrinsic rewards  $r^{E}$  in each environment ( $\lambda$  values are detailed in Appendix A.4.3). Fig. 4 shows the extrinsic return in 6 selected environments given each  $\lambda$  choice. Overall, no choice of  $\lambda$  consistently generates performance improvements over RND. For instance,  $r^{E} \approx \lambda r^{I}$  substantially improves RND in Jamesbond, yet deteriorates RND in YarsRevenge. This shows that the range of acceptable constant  $\lambda$  values is highly environment-dependent, and could be narrow or potentially nonexistent. Moreover, the effect of  $\lambda$  is unpredictable. Intuitively, raising  $\lambda$  increases the weight of intrinsic rewards in the optimization objective and potentially introduces more bias, yet  $r^{E} < \lambda r^{I}$  outperforms  $r^{E} \gg \lambda r^{I}$  in an easy exploration game Jamesbond (based on taxonomy in [2]). In contrast, EIP0 consistently performs better than PPO and RND using  $\lambda = 1$  in all environments, demonstrating that EIP0 is far less susceptible to an ill-tuned  $\lambda$ .

# 5 Discussion

Comparison with Decay-RND Decay-RND requires hand-tuning the decay schedule of  $\lambda$  to control the weighting between extrinsic  $r^{E}$  and intrinsic rewards  $r^{I}$  (i.e.,  $r^{E} + \lambda r^{I}$ ). By contrast,

the Lagrangian multiplier  $\alpha$  in EIPO adjusts the relative importance between both reward functions automatically. Fig. 5 shows that the EIPO-optimized trajectory of  $\alpha$  during training is quite different across environments, indicating that the optimal decay schedule is highly environment dependent. As such, it is unlikely that there exists a single decay schedule that works well across all environments. Additionally, Fig. 5 shows that  $\alpha$  decreases over time and yet still outperforms Decay-RND in a handful of environments (see the learning curve on Carnival in Appendix A.6). This implies that in certain domains it may be better to amplify the intrinsic reward rather than decay it.

Comparison with Decoupled-RND Though Decoupled-RND does not require tuning the decay schedule of  $\lambda$ , the experimental results in Section 4 show that Decoupled-RND does not improve upon Ext-norm-RND, and can even deteriorate Ext-norm-RND on Montezuma's Revenge. We hypothesize that this is because Decoupled-RND cannot adaptively tune the importance of intrinsic and extrinsic rewards during optimization. Decoupled-RND enforces the constraint that the exploration policy  $\pi_{E + I}$  perform similarly to the exploitation policy  $\pi_E$ , but if this constraint excessively penalizes  $\pi_{E + I}$  in the early stages of training,  $\pi_{E + I}$  will tend to degenerate to  $\pi_E$  and lose the exploration incentive generated by  $r^I$ . EIPO can adaptively adjust the trade off between both policies despite enforcing the KL-divergence constraint. Consequently, EIPO loosens the extrinsic optimality constraint at the start of training before tightening it later on. The curve of  $\alpha$  w.r.t. time shown in Appendix A.6 validates our hypothesis, showing that  $\alpha$  decreases first before increasing again in the middle of training.

To conclude, we propose a theoretically motivated framework to mitigate the bias of intrinsic rewards. Our resulting algorithm, EIPO, exhibits consistent performance improvements over PPO while preserving the performance gains of curiosity-driven exploration on hard exploration tasks. Moreover, EIPO is able to adapt the importance of intrinsic rewards during optimization, reducing the need to hand-tune hyperparameters such as exploration schedules ( $\epsilon$ -greedy), or  $\lambda$  decay (Decay-RND). One interesting avenue for future work could be to incorporate intrinsic reward function optimization into our framework, hopefully increasing the flexibility of our method on a range of tasks.
